claims.text: A hybrid framework will couple ab initio calculations with machine-learning corrections.
The hybrid framework will predict temperature-dependent conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than traditional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The modeled bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The specimen has a controlled defect landscape produced under standard processing conditions.
The machine-learning adjustments will explicitly account for scattering associated with oxygen impurities.
Defect scattering dominates conductivity behavior from nearly 0 to 200 K.
Phonon scattering and defect interactions are important from 300 to 1200 K.
The model will be calibrated using samples containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr produces point-defect-related changes in the defect landscape.
Oxygen-induced defects cause local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
The oxygen-induced defect structure modifies electron scattering.
The oxygen-induced defect structure modifies phonon scattering.
Machine learning trained on experimental data can refine descriptors or results derived from ab initio calculations.
The hybrid model will capture nonlinear corrections to carrier scattering.
Explicit treatment of oxygen-related scattering will bridge the gap between defect-free predictions and measurements on oxygen-containing samples.
The model will reduce electrical-conductivity prediction error relative to conventional perfect-crystal models over both temperature regimes.
The model will reduce thermal-conductivity prediction error relative to conventional perfect-crystal models over both temperature regimes.
For the oxygenated specimen, high-temperature conductivity will be approximately 10–15% lower than ideal-crystal analytical estimates.
The claimed accuracy advantage is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and to the intervals of 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Extrapolation beyond the calibrated oxygen level or temperature ranges is uncertain.
